newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries down at midday, Greenspan hawkish.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries down at midday, Greenspan hawkish.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices had backtracked sharply by midday on Wednesday, reacting to what was interpreted as the unexpectedly hawkish tone of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

Greenspan's remarks emphasized that the Fed sees the "distribution of inflation risks skewed to the upside" and said the central bank must remain "especially alert" to the possible emergency of imbalances in financial and product markets that eventually could threaten the current, low-inflation environment.
The market fell sharply at the outset of Greenspan's remarks, trimmed its losses and then headed lower again as it became apparent that the entire text of Greenspan's remarks was cautionary.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond was down 1-7/32, yielding 6.75 percent, by the time Greenspan's question and answer period with the Senate Banking Committee concluded.
"Greenspan talked much tougher than he has recently and so the risk of tighter monetary policy is greater," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Lieberman said the market's retreat was an appropriate reaction to the Fed Chairman's "tougher talk."

Despite the tough-minded nature of the Fed Chairman's remarks, Lieberman said he did not expect the central bank "to pull the trigger" and raise interest rates in the immediate future "without evidence of ongoing strong growth or significant upward pressure on labor costs or something in the pipeline that implies higher inflation."
John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust, said the market sold off in reaction to the Greenspan testimony -- and appropriately so.

"The markets have been overly complacent and Mr. Greenspan is trying to warn them that this ideal world that we've been living in recently might not last forever," said Williams. "It's appropriate for the market to sell-off," Williams said. "The risks of inflation are all to the upside."
But Williams, too, said he believed that the Fed would not rush to raise interest rates.
"Contrary to what Greenspan said about being pre-emptive, I think they really will wait until they see actual inflation pressure (before hiking interest rates)," he said.
The Greenspan testimony concluded before the only other market event of the session -- the Treasury's auction of $12.5 billion in five-year notes.
Analysts said the five-year note sale could attract some demand it might not otherwise have garnered after the price concession prompted by the Greenspan testimony.

"I would guess getting rates up this fast might bring in a little nibbling," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. But Stiles said he felt the five-year maturity is "the wrong place to be on the curve now" if the bias of the market will be for higher rates and coupon curve flattening.
Shortly before the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline for the auction, the five-year notes to be sold then were yielding 6.33 percent on a when-issued basis.

At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates had risen four basis points to 5.06 percent in early afternoon dealings. Six-month rates were up nine basis points to 5.08 percent. Year bill rates were up 10 basis points to 5.30 percent.
Two-year notes were down 9/32 to 99-22/32, yielding 6.04 percent. Ten-year notes were down 29/32 to 98-2/32, yielding 6.52 percent. (( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
